facts.text: Ventricular fibrillation.
Known hypersensitivity to digoxin or any other digitalis preparation (e.g., rash, oral swelling, breathing difficulty).
In patients with Wolff‑Parkinson‑White syndrome who develop atrial fibrillation, digoxin can precipitate rapid ventricular response and ventricular fibrillation.
facts.population: Patients with accessory AV pathway (WPW) and atrial fibrillation

facts.text: Patients with pre‑existing sinus node disease or AV block are at risk for severe sinus bradycardia, sino‑atrial block, or complete heart block; consider pacemaker before therapy.
facts.population: Patients with sinus node disease or AV block

facts.text: Digoxin toxicity manifests as nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, and a wide range of arrhythmias; risk is increased by advanced age, low body weight, impaired renal function, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, or hypomagnesemia.
facts.population: Elderly, low‑weight, renal‑impaired, or electrolyte‑disturbed patients

facts.text: Discontinue or reduce digoxin 1–2 days before electrical cardioversion to avoid ventricular arrhythmias; if cardioversion cannot be delayed, use the lowest possible energy.
Digoxin is not recommended in acute myocardial infarction because it may increase myocardial oxygen demand and precipitate ischemia.
Avoid digoxin in myocarditis; it can cause vasoconstriction and promote pro‑inflammatory cytokine release.

In heart‑failure patients with preserved left‑ventricular systolic function (e.g., restrictive cardiomyopathy, amyloid heart disease, constrictive pericarditis, hypertrophic subaortic stenosis) digoxin may reduce cardiac output and should generally be avoided.
facts.population: Patients with preserved LV systolic function

facts.text: Hypocalcemia can nullify digoxin’s inotropic effect; therapy may be ineffective until calcium is corrected.
Hypothyroidism reduces digoxin requirements; hyperthyroidism, hypermetabolic states, or hyperoxia may render digoxin less effective.
facts.population: Patients with thyroid disorders or hypermetabolic states

facts.text: Initial dosing is individualized based on age, lean body weight, renal function, and concomitant drugs; loading dose (if used) is half the total dose followed by two quarter‑doses 6–8 h apart.
Oral loading dose: 5–10 years = 20–45 µg/kg total; >10 years = 10–15 µg/kg total.

Maintenance dose for adults and children >10 years with normal renal function: 3.4–5.1 µg/kg/day once daily; dose adjustments are made according to lean body weight and creatinine clearance (see dosing tables).
Pediatric maintenance (5–10 years) is 3.2–6.4 µg/kg per dose given twice daily; dosing tables provide adjustments for lean body weight and renal function.
Serum digoxin <0.5 ng/mL may be sub‑therapeutic; >2 ng/mL is associated with toxicity without added benefit. Levels should be drawn just before the next dose (or ≥6 h after the last dose).
When switching from IV to oral digoxin, account for oral bioavailability (60–80%); e.g., 100 µg IV ≈ 125–150 µg oral.
P‑glycoprotein inducers or inhibitors can markedly alter digoxin pharmacokinetics; monitor levels and adjust dose accordingly.

Drugs that increase digoxin concentrations >50 % (e.g., amiodarone, clarithromycin, dronedarone, gentamicin, erythromycin, itraconazole, lapatinib, propafenone, quinidine, ranolazine, ritonavir, telaprevir, tetracycline, verapamil) require a 30–50 % dose reduction and serum level monitoring.

Drugs that increase digoxin concentrations <50 % (e.g., atorvastatin, carvedilol, conivaptan, diltiazem, indomethacin, mirabegron, nefazodone, nifedipine, propantheline, quinine, rabeprazole, saquinavir, spironolactone, telmisartan, ticagrelor, tolvaptan, trimethoprim) generally require a 15–30 % dose reduction.
Drugs that decrease digoxin levels (e.g., acarbose, activated charcoal, antacids, cholestyramine, metoclopramide, rifampin, St. John’s Wort) may require a 20–40 % dose increase.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, and COX‑2 inhibitors can reduce renal clearance of digoxin, increasing serum levels; monitor renal function and digoxin concentrations.

Antiarrhythmics (dofetilide, sotalol, dronedarone) have been associated with increased risk of torsades, pro‑arrhythmia, or sudden death when combined with digoxin; use with caution and monitor closely.
Teriparatide can cause transient hypercalcemia, which may predispose to digoxin toxicity.
Thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism may increase digoxin dose requirements.
Sympathomimetics (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine) can increase the risk of digoxin‑related arrhythmias.
Intravenous calcium administered rapidly can precipitate serious arrhythmias in digoxin‑treated patients.
Beta‑blockers and calcium‑channel blockers have additive AV‑node slowing effects, increasing risk of bradycardia and heart block.
Ivabradine may increase bradycardia risk when combined with digoxin.

Endogenous digoxin‑like immunoreactive substances (DLIS) and some herbal products (e.g., Chan Su, ginseng, Ashwagandha) can cause false‑positive or falsely elevated digoxin assay results; consider alternative assay methods (LC‑MS/MS).

Elderly patients have increased susceptibility to digoxin toxicity due to age‑related decline in renal function, lower lean body mass, and higher likelihood of electrolyte disturbances; start at lower doses and monitor serum levels closely.
Impaired renal function markedly raises digoxin levels; dosing tables adjust maintenance dose according to creatinine clearance (e.g., 10 mL/min → 62.5–125 µg/day).
Drugs that reduce GFR or tubular secretion (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs) can further decrease digoxin clearance and should prompt dose reduction and level monitoring.
